protractor (define it: a tool that measures angles in degrees)

source: Fold a piece of paper and unfold it. Do you see a crease? (T

items.question: Fold a piece of paper and unfold it. Do you see a crease? (This gives the idea of a line segment. It has two end points, A and B.)
steps: Fold the paper and open it.
The crease is straight and has two ends: A and B.
items.answer: Yes, the crease is a straight mark; it gives the idea of a line segment with two end points A and B.

videos.answer: Yes, the crease is a straight mark; it gives the idea of a line segment with two end points A and B.

source: Mark any two points A and B on a sheet of paper. Try to conn

items.question: Mark any two points A and B on a sheet of paper. Try to connect A to B by various routes (Fig. 2.1). What is the shortest route from A to B?
steps: Draw several routes from A to B (zig-zag, curved).
Compare lengths; the straight route is shortest.
This shortest path including A and B is the line segment AB.
items.answer: The straight path from A to B, which is the line segment AB.

videos.answer: The straight path from A to B, which is the line segment AB.

source: Imagine that the line segment AB is extended beyond A in one

items.question: Imagine that the line segment AB is extended beyond A in one direction and beyond B in the other direction without any end (Fig. 2.2). Do you think you can draw a complete picture of a line? No. Why?
steps: A line has no end in either direction.
Paper is finite, so we can draw only a part and put arrows at both ends.
items.answer: No, because a line goes on forever in both directions, so only a part of it can be drawn (arrowheads show it continues).

videos.answer: No, because a line goes on forever in both directions, so only a part of it can be drawn (arrowheads show it continues).

source: A torch at T shines a beam towards a lamp post L. The beam g

items.question: A torch at T shines a beam towards a lamp post L. The beam goes past L and never stops. Is the beam a line segment, a ray or a line? Name it.
steps: The beam starts at T, a fixed starting point.
It passes through L and goes on in one direction without end.
A part of a line with one starting point is a ray.
The starting point comes first in the name, so the beam is ray TL.
items.answer: It is a ray, named TL, with starting point T.

videos.answer: It is a ray, named TL, with starting point T.

items.question: Rihan marked a point on a piece of paper. How many lines can he draw that pass through the point? Sheetal marked two points on a piece of paper. How many different lines can she draw that pass through both of the points? Can you help Rihan and Sheetal find their answers? Rihan) How many lines can be drawn through one marked point? Sheetal) How many different lines through both of two marked points?
steps: Through one point, lines can point in any direction, so there are endlessly many.
Two points determine a unique line.
items.answer: Rihan: many (uncountably many) lines. Sheetal: only one line.

videos.answer: Rihan: many (uncountably many) lines. Sheetal: only one line.

items.question: Name the line segments in Fig. 2.4. Which of the five marked points are on exactly one of the line segments? Which are on two of the line segments? (Fig. 2.4 is a zig-zag path L-M-P-Q-R: L to M, M to P, P to Q, Q to R.) a) Name the line segments. b) Points on exactly one segment c) Points on two segments
steps: Each straight piece between consecutive marked points is a segment.
End points L and R belong to one piece each.
M, P, Q are joints shared by two pieces.
items.answer: Segments LM, MP, PQ, QR. L and R are on exactly one segment; M, P and Q are on two segments.

items.question: Here is a ray OA (Fig. 2.7). It starts at O and passes through the point A. It also passes through the point B. a. Can you also name it as OB? Why? b. Can we write OA as AO? Why or why not? a) Can you also name it as OB? Why? b) Can we write OA as AO? Why or why not?
steps: A ray is named by its starting point first, then any other point on it.
OA and OB start at O and go the same way, so they are the same ray.
AO starts at A, so it is a different ray.
items.answer: a) Yes, the ray starts at O and B is on it. b) No, AO would start at A.

source: Vidya opens the cover of her book in six cases (Case 1 to Ca

items.question: Vidya opens the cover of her book in six cases (Case 1 to Case 6). Do you see angles being made in each of these cases? Can you mark their arms and vertex?
steps: The book cover and the page below it form the two arms.
The vertex is the hinge where they join.
items.answer: Yes, an angle is formed in each case. The arms are the cover and the rest of the book (the two rays along the cover and the book); the vertex is the hinge/spine where they meet.

videos.answer: Yes, an angle is formed in each case. The arms are the cover and the rest of the book (the two rays along the cover and the book); the vertex is the hinge/spine where they meet.

source: In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle.

items.question: In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle. The vertex is the point where the two arms are joined. Identify the arms and vertex of the angle.
steps: The two legs are the arms.
The joint where they meet is the vertex.
items.answer: The two legs of the compass are the arms; the vertex is the joint (hinge) at the top where the arms are joined.

videos.answer: The two legs of the compass are the arms; the vertex is the joint (hinge) at the top where the arms are joined.

source: A pair of scissors has two blades. When we open them (or 'tu

items.question: A pair of scissors has two blades. When we open them (or 'turn them') to cut something, the blades form an angle. Identify the arms and the vertex of the angle.
steps: The blades are the arms.
The pivot screw is the vertex.
items.answer: The two blades are the arms; the vertex is the screw/pivot where the blades are joined.

videos.answer: The two blades are the arms; the vertex is the screw/pivot where the blades are joined.

source: Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common

items.question: Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common objects (a stapler, a hinged box, a box with an open flap). Identify the angles in them by marking out their arms and vertices.
steps: Find the two parts that turn about a hinge.
Those parts are the arms; the hinge is the vertex.
items.answer: Each object has two parts joined at a hinge; the two parts are the arms and the hinge is the vertex (e.g., spectacles: a temple (side arm) and the frame; wallet: the two halves; stapler: the top and base; box: lid and box).

videos.answer: Each object has two parts joined at a hinge; the two parts are the arms and the hinge is the vertex (e.g., spectacles: a temple (side arm) and the frame; wallet: the two halves; stapler: the top and base; box: lid and box).

steps: The size of an angle is the amount of rotation.
In Case 2 the cover is rotated more than in Case 1.
items.answer: The angle in Case 2 is greater, because she needs to rotate the cover more.

Draw ray ST and ray SR from S.
Mark a small curve between them.

items.question: Explain why ∠APB cannot be labelled as ∠P. (Figure: vertex P with three rays going through A (upper), B (middle) and C (lower).)
steps: At P there are three rays, PA, PB, PC.
So there are three different angles at P.
∠P alone cannot tell which one; use points on both arms.
items.answer: Three angles share the vertex P (∠APB, ∠BPC and ∠APC). Naming one as ∠P would not say which of them is meant, so we must name a point on each arm.

videos.answer: Three angles share the vertex P (∠APB, ∠BPC and ∠APC). Naming one as ∠P would not say which of them is meant, so we must name a point on each arm.

Each point is a vertex of one angle, giving 3 angles.

items.question: Now consider ∠AOB and ∠XOY in the figure. Which is greater?
steps: Superimpose the angles with O on O.
Arm OA falls on OX and OB falls on OY.
So the two angles are equal.
items.answer: Neither. The angles are equal in size, because when superimposed the vertex O and the arms OA with OX and OB with OY lie on top of each other.

source: Where else do we use superimposition to compare?

steps: Place one shape over another to compare size.
items.answer: A few examples are line segments, squares and circles. Think of more.

source: Is it always easy to compare two angles?

items.question: Is it always easy to compare two angles?
steps: Angles with nearly the same opening look alike.
We need superimposition (or measuring) to be sure.
items.answer: No. It is not always easy to compare two angles; for example angles of 89 degrees and 91 degrees cannot be compared without measuring or overlapping. For the given figures, comparison is easy.

videos.answer: No. It is not always easy to compare two angles; for example angles of 89 degrees and 91 degrees cannot be compared without measuring or overlapping. For the given figures, comparison is easy.

source: A transparent circle is placed on the angle of the first cra

items.question: A transparent circle is placed on the angle of the first crane with its centre at the vertex; A and B are marked where the arms cross the circle. The circle is then placed on the second crane's angle with the vertex at the centre and one arm through OA. Can you now tell which angle is bigger?
steps: Match one arm of each angle with OA.
Compare the other end points on the circle (B and Y).
A farther end point means a bigger angle.
items.answer: Compare where the second arm meets the circle, at Y, with the point B. If Y is beyond B the second angle is bigger, if Y falls on B they are equal, and if Y falls short of B it is smaller. Here Y is very close to B, so the two angles are nearly equal.

videos.answer: Compare where the second arm meets the circle, at Y, with the point B. If Y is beyond B the second angle is bigger, if Y falls on B they are equal, and if Y falls short of B it is smaller. Here Y is very close to B, so the two angles are nearly equal.

source: Which crane was making the bigger angle? If you can make a c

items.question: Which crane was making the bigger angle? If you can make a circular piece of transparent paper, try this method to compare the angles in Fig. 2.10 with each other.
steps: Place the circle's centre on the vertex of each crane's angle.
Mark A and B where the arms cross the circle.
Slide the circle to the other angle, keep one arm on OA, and compare where the other arm crosses.
items.answer: Trace both beak angles, place the transparent circle on each with its centre on the vertex, mark where the arms cross, and compare the gaps between the marked points on the circle. The crane whose arms are further apart makes the bigger angle.

videos.answer: Trace both beak angles, place the transparent circle on each with its centre on the vertex, mark where the arms cross, and compare the gaps between the marked points on the circle. The crane whose arms are further apart makes the bigger angle.

Make different angles by folding a rectangular sheet of paper and compare the angles. Which is the largest and smallest angle you made?
steps: Fold the sheet and mark the crease.
Name the four angles between the crease and the sides.
Compare by superimposition or folding.
items.answer: Example from the book: a slanting crease EF from E on one long side to F on the opposite side gives the angles ∠AEF, ∠BEF, ∠DFE, ∠CFE. ∠AEF and ∠CFE are larger than ∠BEF and ∠DFE. Try more cases; the largest and smallest depend on the folds you make.

source: Collect a number of rotating arms with different angles (do

items.question: Collect a number of rotating arms with different angles (do not rotate any of them). Take a cardboard and make an angle-shaped slit by tracing and cutting out the shape of one of the rotating arms. Now shuffle and mix up all the rotating arms. Can you identify which of the rotating arms will pass through the slit?
steps: Place an arm over the slit.
If the slit angle is greater than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
If the slit angle is less than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
If equal, the arms go through.
items.answer: Only the arm whose angle is equal to the slit's angle passes through; place each over the slit to find it. Passing through depends only on the angle, not on the arms' lengths (as long as they are shorter than the slit).

videos.answer: Only the arm whose angle is equal to the slit's angle passes through; place each over the slit to find it. Passing through depends only on the angle, not on the arms' lengths (as long as they are shorter than the slit).

source: Challenge: Reduce this angle. (A girl snips the ends of the

items.question: Challenge: Reduce this angle. (A girl snips the ends of the arms of a V-shaped rotating arm with scissors: 'Angle reduced.' The boy says 'The angle is still the same!')
steps: Cutting shortens the arms but the opening stays the same.
To reduce the angle, rotate one arm closer to the other.
items.answer: Cutting the arms shorter does not change the angle; the size of an angle depends only on the amount of turn between the arms, not on their length. To reduce the angle, bring the arms closer together (turn one arm).

videos.answer: Cutting the arms shorter does not change the angle; the size of an angle depends only on the amount of turn between the arms, not on their length. To reduce the angle, bring the arms closer together (turn one arm).

steps: Mark A, O, B on one edge.
Fold so OB falls on OA.

source: Justify why the two angles are equal. Is there a way to supe

items.question: Justify why the two angles are equal. Is there a way to superimpose and check? Can this superimposition be done by folding?
steps: Fold along crease OC.
OA and OB coincide, so ∠AOC fits on ∠COB.
So they are equal.
items.answer: Because OB was folded onto OA, the two arms overlap exactly, so the two angles fit exactly on each other and are equal. Yes, folding itself is the superimposition: fold along the crease and the two angles coincide.

items.question: If a straight angle is formed by half of a full turn, how much of a full turn will form a right angle?

Half of half a turn = 1/4 of a full turn.
items.answer: 1/4 of a full turn (a quarter turn).

items.question: The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes. What is the degree measure of the angle between two spokes next to each other? What is the largest acute angle formed between two spokes?
steps: Multiples of 15 below 90 are 15, 30, 45, 60, 75; the largest is 75
items.answer: 15° between neighbouring spokes; the largest acute angle between two spokes is 75°.

items.question: Puzzle: I am an acute angle. If you double my measure, you get an acute angle. If you triple my measure, you will get an acute angle again. If you quadruple (four times) my measure, you will get an acute angle yet again! But if you multiply my measure by 5, you will get an obtuse angle measure. What are the possibilities for my measure?
steps: 4 × measure < 90, so measure < 22.5
5 × measure > 90, so measure > 18
Whole degrees between 18 and 22.5: 19, 20, 21, 22
items.answer: The acute angle can be 19°, 20°, 21° and 22° (whole-number degrees).

videos.answer: The acute angle can be 19°, 20°, 21° and 22° (whole-number degrees).
